01

The four tables

Each card is one table. Columns are listed with their SQL type; PK is the primary key, FK points at another table, and JSON columns store a whole JSON value as text — that's what lets each row round-trip 1:1 with the JSON objects below.

households 1 row

idTEXTPKhse_cd6e2266
nameTEXT"Mann"
created_atTEXTISO timestamp

users 1 row

idTEXTPKusr_…
emailTEXTUNIQUEsign-in identity

household_idTEXTFK → households
roleTEXTowner | member
saved_recipesTEXTJSON [ids]the cookbook
favorite_recipesTEXTJSON [ids]
uploaded_recipesTEXTJSON [ids]
recipe_ratingsTEXTJSON {id → 1–5}
preferencesTEXTJSON object
created_at / updated_atTEXT

recipes 3 rows

owner_idTEXT · nullableFK → usersNULL = house-shared
nameTEXT

ingredientsTEXTJSON [{name, display}]

prep_time / cook_timeTEXTfree text, e.g. "15 min"
servingsINTEGER

created_at / updated_atTEXT

idTEXTPKplan_…
household_idTEXTFK → households

How they connect

  • users.household_id→ a user belongs to exactly one household
  • recipes.owner_id→ who uploaded it — or NULL, meaning a house-shared seed anyone in the household sees
  • week_plans.household_id→ the plan belongs to the household, not a person — one plan per household per week
  • users.saved_recipes / favorite_recipes / uploaded_recipes→ lists of recipe ids — pointers into the recipes table, never copies of recipes

03

The three recipes

All three rows in recipes, in full. Two things worth your eye: every ingredient is stored as a pair — name (bare, for pantry matching) and display (the full shopping-list text) — and category is null on all three, because neither source file recorded one. Nothing was invented to fill it.

04

The week plan

One row in week_plans: the Mann household's plan for the week starting Monday, Oct 19, 2026. It's real and it's empty — that's the current state, not a mockup. The second view shows the shape of a filled plan, taken from the automated test run: a throwaway week that was created, filled, verified, and then deleted.

Stored plan — week of Mon Oct 19, 2026plan_fe7e7d85 · householdId hse_cd6e2266

Potential meals — the bucket

Empty. Meals land here first (from a recipe card's calendar-plus button, or as a typed menu item), then get placed into a day.

An entry is one of two shapes: { "type": "recipe", "recipeId": "minestrone" } { "type": "menuItem", "name": "Pizza night" } Placing a meal moves it — out of the bucket, into the slot.

06

Not in the database yet

The pantry table

The one remaining table. Elizabeth's inventory (146 items across the freezers, fridge, and pantry) isn't stored yet. The plan is to key it to the household, not to you — the inventory is the household's. The recipe ingredients' bare name field is what pantry matching will compare against.

Names change between JSON and SQL

The JSON objects use camelCase (savedRecipes, weekStartsOn); the SQL columns use snake_case (saved_recipes, week_start). Same data, two spellings — worth knowing when you read either side.

Snapshot of ~/workspace/meal-planner-db/mealplanner.db as exported Oct 24, 2026. Dish photos are representative of the named recipes; the database itself stores only an image path (/images/minestrone.jpg etc.). If anything on this page looks wrong, that's the review working — say the word and the database changes.
